A while back, a Ugandan pastor said marriage isn't a must for ministers.
Singleness, he argued, offers self-discovery and spiritual maturity and the church should stop pressuring pastors to marry.
Is your single pastor automatically a problem? No.
The question isn't whether a single man can be godly or fruitful.
It's what the apostles expected when they described the man fit to pastor.
Paul says a pastor must be "a one-woman man" that's about character, not a marriage certificate.
But he immediately adds that a pastor must manage his own household well because if he can't run his family, how will he care for God's church?
The household is God's proving ground for shepherds.
So marriage isn't a magic checkbox.
That's why the single candidate should be the outlier the burden of proof is on him.
What about Paul? He was single but he calls his celibacy a rare, extraordinary gift.
Luther said one in a thousand.
A single man burning with passion isn't gifted; he's a ticking time bomb.
So: character is the real qualification but ordinarily, look for a husband and a father.
